messages.subject: Re: interpretation of half-normal detection function
messages.body_plain:
Hi Laura
The detection function describes the probability that an individual will be detected at a particular detector on a particular occasion. The further apart are the animal's activity centre and the detector, the lower the probability. Animal activity centres are not observed, and distances are not observed; all we have are detection histories (patterns) of observed individuals, but these are sufficient to fit the (implicit) model by maximising the likelihood. As you suggest, this is based on recaptures within the data, in that detection histories with multiple observations provide information on the spatial scale of detection (sigma). The parameters g0 and sigma jointly define the detection function. It's common for g0 to be small - remember it relates to a single detector on a single occasion.
Murray

Murray

As always, thank you for the response! Good to know that it is common for g0 to be small – that makes me feel better.

Should it converge at some point, at which then we would know it is sufficiently small?

Specifically, several of the trap lines do not have any contour lines around them (pic attached). It does not seem to be related to the # of captures/recaptures since some of the trap lines that had no captures still have contour lines around them. Could you help me understand why some trap lines have contours and others do not? Is it something that I should be concerned about?

Much appreciated and looking forward to hearing from you,

Laura

messages.body_plain:
Good day Laura,
If, when you reduced spacing, you didn't increase the total number of points in the mask, then the extent of the mask will shrink.  If the extent of the mask is too small, density estimates will be sensitive to the extent. Make sure you're keeping the extent the same when you reduce spacing (which perhaps you are; this is just a guess as to what might have happenned).
Eric

messages.body_plain:
Hi Elsa

I would (and do) avoid 3-class models. The help for 'hcov says

"In general hcov has been designed for two classes and two classes are assumed if neither ‘h2’ nor ‘h3’ appears in the model formulae. However, there is a small exception: hcov may have three non-missing levels if ‘h3’ appears in a model formula. Note that h2 cannot be combined with h3; h3 is for advanced use only and has not been fully tested."

That was a copout on my part - there are enough problems with mixture models that I haven't been motivated to fully test and implement h3. The link for h3 has to ensure the components sum to 1; secr uses a variation on mlogit as in MARK, but its implementation is a pain.

I don't follow where your 'pmix logit' values are coming from. It might help to see the secr.fit and predict statements that you are using. I would expect you can get good estimates of density without exhaustively modelling variation in sigma (and modelling sigma alone may make matters worse, given that g0 is likely to vary inversely).

Lack of SE does generally indicate fitting problems or an attempt to estimate a parameter at a boundary. Numerical problems can sometimes be overcome by re-running secr.fit with method = "none" and start = first.fit (the name of the saved first fit); this just re-estimates the SE (using a different and slightly more sophisticated algorithm). At least that check is much faster than re-fitting the model.

With finite mixtures there is a good chance of getting stuck on a local maximum of the likelihood - this might explain erratic results of AIC model selection (and contributes to my frustration with the method in general).

I'm sorry these comments won't really solve your problem. The topic could use some deeper investigation. Meantime, I would stick to simple, robust models and avoid those that are problematic to fit. AIC isn't everything.
Murray

messages.body_plain:
Hi again

I don't see a problem when I fit these models. Are you using secr 3.1.0? The estimates come out at 14 /100 km^2 (95%CI 8-23/100 km^2), which is almost too good to be true (vs your previous estimate). (Multiply animals/ha by 10000 to get animals/100km^2).  It's a mistake to apply derived(). Admittedly the warning message "use of allsighting here untested" should be stronger - an outright error.

The arguments of sightingPlot need to be tuned to get a useful plot:

sightingPlot(ResightJanApr17CH, type = "Tu", mean = FALSE,

    gridsp = 1000, border = 4000, dropunused = FALSE, fill = FALSE, scale = 200)

As you probably realise, the newdata argument in predict specifies a predictor 'ts' that is not in the particular model (all occasions are sighting occasions). The sighting-only estimate is making a strong assumption: uniform distribution of marked animals across the habitat mask (buffered area) so I don't see why you would bother with this model if you have the marking data.

Murray
